title: Personal Agent Protocol: discover, sign in, call the API
lede: A personal agent identified by a URL starts from a Company origin, pushes its sign-in request to PingFederate (PAR), lets the person sign in, then signs every request with a Poppy-Session. Solid arrows are what the agent (or the person's browser) sends, dashed arrows are the answers; press Simulate and each step explains itself.

steps.title: Discover the Company origin
steps.what: The agent reads /.well-known/poppy.json and /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource from the one origin you typed. Two public GETs, no identity yet, and no redirects followed.
steps.why: This is how an agent starts from a Company origin it has never seen. Nothing is configured on the agent side: the Company's own documents say what it offers and where to sign in.

steps.title: The Company origin answers
steps.what: poppy.json gives the protocol version (1.0 here), the scopes, each with a scope_hint, the issuer and the APIs. The agent checks the version is compatible (same major), the domain is the host, and the resource is exactly the origin.
steps.why: scope_hints say whether a scope changes anything or touches personal data, so the agent can tell the person what they are about to allow. The exact-resource rule stops one Company's document from speaking for another resource on the same host.

steps.title: Push the sign-in request (PAR)
steps.what: The issuer's metadata lists a pushed_authorization_request_endpoint, so the agent POSTs the whole sign-in request there: scope, redirect, PKCE challenge and state, with a client assertion signed by its private key (private_key_jwt). Its client_id is the URL of its own metadata document (CIMD).
steps.why: The authorization server knows which agent is asking before the person sees any page, and it fetches the agent's client.json from that URL, so it never holds a stale copy of the agent's keys or redirect address (PingFederate still needs an operator-made CIMD policy for that exact URL). FAPI 2.0 Companies require PAR (RFC 9126).

steps.title: A one-time request_uri
steps.what: PingFederate stores the pushed request and answers 201 with a short-lived request_uri.
steps.why: Nothing in the browser can change the request now: the address the person opens carries only client_id and this reference.

steps.title: The person signs in
steps.what: The browser opens the authorization endpoint with just client_id and request_uri. The person signs in on the Company's own page and presses Allow for this agent and this scope.
steps.why: The only step the person sees. They never hand the agent a password, and the consent names the agent by its URL, so they can revoke it like any other app.

steps.title: The code comes back
steps.what: PingFederate redirects to the agent's /cb with a one-time code and its iss. The agent checks the state, and that iss is the issuer it started with (RFC 9207).
steps.why: The iss check stops a mix-up attack, where a code from another authorization server is played back to the agent.

steps.title: Exchange the code
steps.what: The agent POSTs the code, the PKCE verifier and a fresh client assertion to the token endpoint.
steps.why: PKCE proves the agent that started the sign-in is the one finishing it; the assertion proves it holds the key published at its jwks_uri. There is no client secret anywhere.

steps.title: The access token
steps.what: The token comes back with client_id set to the agent's URL, the person as sub, and the scope that was granted.
steps.why: Every API the Company runs can now tell agent traffic from a person's, and exactly which agent it is.

steps.title: Call the API
steps.what: GET /poppy/api/v1/me with the Bearer token and two more headers: Poppy-Session, a JWT signed for this one request by a short-lived delegated key (the delegation, signed by the agent's key, rides inside it as poppy_dlg), and Poppy-Version: 1.0.
steps.why: The token says what the person allowed; the session says which agent is asking right now, for this method, this URL and this token. A stolen token alone is not enough.

steps.title: The Company verifies
steps.what: It checks the token, then the session: the delegation against the agent's jwks_uri, the session signature, method and URL, the token hash (ath), a fresh jti, and the version. Then it answers 200 with who the agent acts for.
steps.why: A replayed session, one signed for another token, or an unsupported version gets 400 (invalid_session or version_unsupported), and an agent the Company has not allow-listed is refused.
